legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Can LLMs Ask Good Questions?" Yueheng Zhang*, Xiaoyuan Liu* (equal contribution), Yiyou Sun, Atheer Alharbi, Hend Alzahrani, Tianneng Shi, Basel Alomair, Dawn Song. Affiliations: UC Berkeley, KACST, and the University of Washington (Alomair). arXiv:2501.03491v2, cs.CL, 17 Jun 2025, marked "Preprint". No venue. Code: github.com/CoLearn-Dev/llmqg.

COVERAGE: All 15 pages and 46,680 chars were read. The extraction was in two pieces (0–40,000 and 41,500–end). The skipped 1,500 chars sit inside the reference list. Figures 2–5 are plots with no extractable data, so their content is not reported. Their captions were read, but I did not render the images.

CORE CLAIM: Without extra prompt constraints, LLM-generated questions differ from human ones in measurable ways. LLMs ask more descriptive, fact-and-figure questions that need longer answers. Their question lengths vary less, and they spread over the context more evenly than the human position bias toward the start. The authors say LLM-written questions are therefore useful for testing RAG and detecting hallucination. They also say they offer an automatic six-metric workflow for judging question quality.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- LLMs skew toward descriptive questions, while human sets almost never ask them.
  number: T8 Descriptive is 27.1 (Llama), 44.7 (DeepSeek), 29.4 (Claude) and 37.1 (GPT-4o), against 3.0 (TriviaQA) and 1.5 (HotpotQA). T5 Specific fact/figure is 18.3–30.5 for LLMs against 10.5 and 9.5.
  setup: WikiText contexts. Each LLM wrote 1,024 questions from a shared 256 contexts (N=4), temperature 0. A GPT-4o judge assigned the types. The 10 types were hand-built by inductive coding.
  quote: "T8 Descriptive/Characterization 3.0 1.5 27.1 44.7 29.4 37.1"
  where: Table 1, p.6
- Humans ask identity and attribution questions much more often.
  number: T1 is 34.2 (TriviaQA) and 39.7 (HotpotQA), against 9.3–14.8 for LLMs.
  quote: "T1 Identity/Attribution 34.2 39.7 12.9 9.3 14.8 11.2"
  where: Table 1, p.6
- LLM answers need much more text than human gold answers, and shortening does not close the gap.
  number: Gold answers are 2.0 ± 1.8 words (TriviaQA) and 2.2 ± 1.8 (HotpotQA). LLM answers with context run 24.4–35.0 words. After shortening they are still 7.3–13.7 words.
  setup: Shortening used a concise-answer prompt and word caps of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8. A shorter answer counted if the GPT-4o judge gave it the same 0–5 rating as the original. Standard deviations are large.
  quote: "DeepSeek-V3 35.0 ± 18.7 13.7 ± 19.1"
  where: Table 4, p.9
- Question length is similar across LLMs but less variable than in human sets.
  number: LLMs average 15.3–23.6 words with SD 3.6–5.6. HotpotQA is 18.0 ± 10.0 and TriviaQA 14.0 ± 6.5.
  quote: "HotpotQA 18.0 ± 10.0 / Llama-3.3 23.6 ± 5.6"
  where: Table 2, p.7. See the inconsistencies below for the Llama figure.
- Context coverage is slightly lower for LLMs than for HotpotQA.
  number: Covered words are 33.6% (HotpotQA) against 26.6–32.0% (LLMs). Covered sentences are 31.1% against 26.6–30.4%.
  setup: The sentences relevant to each question were chosen by an LLM judge. Contexts are about 140 words (HotpotQA 139.1, WikiText 140.3).
  quote: "HotpotQA 139.1 ± 53.3 33.6 ± 17.5 6.5 ± 2.5 31.1 ± 15.6"
  where: Table 3, p.7
- LLM questions are spread more evenly across the context, with a slight dip at both ends. Human questions cluster near the start.
  number: none (Figure 2 only)
  quote: "human-generated questions tend to focus on the beginning of the context, likely due to the labeling process. LLM-generated questions exhibit a more balanced distribution, with a slight decrease in focus at both ends."
  where: p.7
- The judge agrees reasonably well with humans.
  number: Pearson 0.76.
  setup: 300 manual annotations, with no annotator count, agreement or method given. GPT-4o judged all four generators.
  quote: "from a sample of 300 manual annotations, the GPT-4o judge achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.76"
  where: p.7
- Removing the context hurts answer quality, and the authors present this as an uncommonness signal.
  number: "about one-fourth" of questions cannot be answered properly without context. "No zero-rating answers are found."
  quote: "Notably, about one-fourth of the generated questions cannot be properly answered."
  where: p.7, Figure 3. The "higher than HotpotQA" comparison is shown only in the plot.
- The results hold across three prompt wordings.
  number: For DeepSeek, T8 is 44.7, 45.6 and 49.3 for v1, v2 and v3. LLM question-length SDs stay at 3.6–4.6 across wordings.
  quote: "the distribution of different question types remains stable, consistently showing that the LLMs prefer descriptive questions."
  where: App. A, Tables 5–6, p.13
- The cost of the whole evaluation is small.
  number: about 70k chat completions, about 2 hours.
  quote: "the complete evaluation uses around 70k chat completion calls, which takes around 2 hours to run."
  where: p.6

MODELS: GPT-4o-2024-08-06, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and DeepSeek-V3 (labelled DeepSeek-V3-0324 in the Figure 3 caption and Table 6). Temperature was 0 with one run each. Open models ran on TogetherAI. The judge was GPT-4o throughout.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- Llama-3.3 question length is 23.6 ± 5.6 in Table 2 but 18.5 ± 4.6 in Table 6 v1. v1 is the main prompt, so the two should match. The text says Llama "generating longer questions".
- The GPT-4o type shares in Table 2 and Table 4 are T1–T5 45.8% and T8–T10 53.4%. Table 6 v1 gives 58.0% and 41.2% for the same group. Table 1 sums to about 45.1% and 53.2%, so Table 6 is the odd one out.
- GPT-4o T9 is 14.1 in Table 1 but 14.7 in Table 5 v1. The two tables should be identical for v1.
- The text says the three-variant check covers "three variations", but v1 is the main prompt, so only two are independent.
- Table 4 shortened-answer SDs exceed the means (for example 7.3 ± 12.6), so the distributions are heavily skewed.
- The Appendix B text cites "Figure 5c" for all question types, but there are three panels.
- The text says "DeepSeek and ChatGPT" prefer descriptive questions even more strongly, and the table agrees. Claude (29.4) and Llama (27.1) are close to each other.
- The abstract says "two open-source and two proprietary", and the text calls them "closed-source". Minor.

LIMITS
- Stated: no reasoning models (o3, R1). Prompt design and preference effects are unexplored. Human alignment was checked only on a small sample, with no Mechanical Turk. No downstream tasks (RAG, hallucination detection) were run. No specialised domains such as finance or medicine.
- Unstated:
  - The human and LLM contexts differ. HotpotQA uses multi-paragraph evidence, and WikiText is a single paragraph with a section title. Human and LLM question sets are not generated from the same contexts, and TriviaQA is excluded from the coverage and answer-quality comparisons. Question-type differences are therefore confounded with task design and the annotation brief.
  - The "never classified" rate is reported as 0.0, but the classifier is an LLM judge with no accuracy given.
  - The question-type classifier, context-coverage selector and answer rater are all GPT-4o. GPT-4o also generates questions, and the self-preference check is only anecdotal ("there isn't a clear difference", no numbers).
  - One run per model with temperature 0, and no confidence intervals or significance tests.
  - The claim that LLM questions suit RAG and hallucination testing is asserted, not tested. A question that the model cannot answer without context may reflect rare knowledge, a vague question or the judge itself.
  - "Good questions" is never defined by human preference or by downstream use, so the title overstates the findings.
  - The paper reports no relation between its metrics and how well questions discriminate between systems.
  - The default prompt asks for "self-contained" questions, which may itself push toward descriptive ones.
  - Claude-3.7 and the other model versions have since dated.

BUILDS ON: Es et al. 2023 (RAGAS: faithfulness, answer relevance, context relevance, sentence-level context measure). Yang et al. 2018 (HotpotQA, question-start heuristics). Joshi et al. 2017 (TriviaQA). Kwiatkowski et al. 2019 (Natural Questions). Saito et al. 2024 (position bias in QA). Wang et al. 2023a (star-rating judge prompts). Fu et al. 2023 (GPTScore), Gorgun and Bulut 2024 (QG evaluation taxonomy), Guo et al. 2024 (QG survey), Wang et al. 2023b (Self-instruct). Related synthetic-data work: ToolQA, HAGRID, ToxiGen, Cosmopedia, BeaverTails, TinyStories.

NOTE FIT (generative-ai/08-eval/notes/03-eval-datasets.md)
- The note is 52,155 chars. It has no existing citation of this paper (grep for "Zhang" and "2501.03491" found only unrelated papers).
- Best fit: "### Synthetic data done right" (line 95) under "## Where tasks come from". That section covers dimension-first generation, mutation toward the edges, the diversity cost of pushing a generator toward failures (Perez et al.), template-built items (BigToM), and the self-preference trap. It lacks evidence on what unconstrained "write N questions about this passage" produces. This paper would supply it: a 37–45% descriptive share against 1.5–3% in the human sets, and answers about 12–15 times longer than gold answers. That supports the section's warning against "100 test questions". It would be a measured, though narrow, version of the "100 variations of the same polite question" claim.
- A second candidate is the Synthetic row in the "Where tasks come from" table ("Tropes, unrealistic phrasing").
- 07-evaluating-rag-and-grounding.md may fit better for the "question generation for RAG testing and hallucination detection" angle, since the paper cites RAGAS. I did not read that note, so check it first.
- Cite with its caveats: single paragraphs, Wikipedia, GPT-4o as the sole judge, one run, 2025 models.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Table 1 is the clearest, a question-type distribution for two human sets against four LLMs, with a bar chart option. Figure 1 (p.2) shows the whole pipeline on one example, including the 36 → 26 word shortening. Figure 3 (rating distributions with and without context) is a plot I could not read.

PROBLEMS: The PDF contains no embedded instructions. Table 3 extracted with Llama's row split across lines, and the DeepSeek, Claude and GPT rows lack the context word and sentence counts (shared, per the caption). Figures 2–5 content is unreadable from text.
